text:
Recent work favors auditing atomic claims against evidence rather than scoring explanation fluency. [Kabongo and Guigue (2025/2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24366) find high semantic similarity can coexist with very low factual precision in recommendation explanations. Their evidence comes from reviews, unavailable here; transfer the statement-level audit method using only histories, titles, and descriptions. Proposed labels: supported match, explicit textual conflict, insufficient evidence. Attach evidence spans to each judgment. Historical interaction supports observed interest; equipment ownership, compatibility, satisfied needs, and current intent remain unknown without explicit support.

[Sufficient Context (2024/ICLR 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.06037) distinguishes evidence sufficiency from model confidence and combines them for selective answering. Applied here, abstain from unsupported compatibility or intent judgments rather than treating missing evidence as rejection. Report coverage—the fraction receiving supported/conflict judgments—alongside error among judged cases and the insufficient-evidence rate, separately by category and claim type. These are proposed audit measures, not established predictors of recommendation HR@10.

[JUDGE-BENCH (2025)](https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-short.20/) shows judge agreement varies substantially across tasks; [Netflix’s 2026 recommendation-explanation study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.18300) emphasizes human-labeled benchmarks and ongoing alignment monitoring. For the twenty-user audit, independently double-annotate a category-balanced sample; report raw agreement, nominal κ or Krippendorff’s α, label counts, and adjudicated disagreements. Compare matched broad-versus-specific recommendations for the same user, randomize presentation order, and permit ties/unknowns. Treat these comparisons as exploratory: establish reliable evidence judgments and validation HR@10 gains before converting qualitative feedback into training objectives.
